description_full: The J. M. Smucker Company manufactures and markets branded food and beverage products worldwide. The company operates through five segments: U.S. Retail Coffee, U.S. Retail Frozen Handheld and Spreads, U.S. Retail Pet Foods, Sweet Baked Snacks, and Away From Home. It offers coffee, sweet baked goods, pet snacks, frozen handheld products, peanut butter, cat and dog food, fruit and specialty spreads, cookies, frozen sandwiches and snacks, hot beverages, portion control products, toppings and syrups, baking mixes and ingredients, and flour. The company provides its products under the Folgers, Café Bustelo, Dunkin', Jif, Smucker's, Uncrustables, Meow Mix, Milk-Bone, Pup-Peroni, Canine Carry Outs, Hostess, and 1850 brand names. It sells its products through direct sales and brokers to food retailers, club stores, discount and dollar stores, online retailers, pet specialty stores, distributors, drug stores, military commissaries, mass merchandisers, supermarket chains, national mass retailers, convenience stores, vending channels, and foodservice distributors and operators. The J. M. Smucker Company was founded in 1897 and is headquartered in Orrville, Ohio.

financial_summary: The J.M. Smucker Company is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $14.2B market cap on $9.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, with gross margins sitting at 37%.
The business throws off $1.2B in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 9.9× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 9.6×.

Shareholder yield of 3.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.3% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
